name: The Good Food Institute (Giving Green, 2026)
summary: Research funding, policy advocacy and industry support for alternative proteins. A re-implementation of Giving Green's estimate of what GFI's work from 2016 to 2022 cost per tonne of CO₂e kept out of the air, through a higher chance that alternative proteins become cheap enough to replace some livestock.

sections.title: From cost per tonne to tonnes per dollar
sections.explainer: charityevals' step after Giving Green's bottom line: Giving Green reports dollars per tonne; the site needs tonnes per dollar, and how much air pollution those tonnes cut. The tonnes are livestock emissions (methane, nitrous oxide and land clearing), not fuel burned, so they count for their heat deaths, discounted over the decades until they come (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

sections.title: Staff pay below market
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not Giving Green's: with credit by share of resources on, staff's pay below what they could earn elsewhere counts as an in-kind contribution and gets its share of the outcome. Off by default.

rows.label: GFI's budget, 2016–2022
rows.explainer: GFI's spending in each year from 2016 to 2022 added up: $3.0 million in 2016 rising to $21.6 million in 2019, then $18.9 million (2020), $14 million (2021) and $30 million (2022, Giving Green's figure). Giving Green divides the whole budget by the emissions GFI's work is expected to avoid after 2022, assuming no further work after 2022.

rows.label: Difference in livestock production between the adjusted low- and high-innovation scenarios (million tonnes, summed over the years until they converge)
rows.explainer: How much less meat and milk is produced in a world where alternative proteins get the research money they need, summed year by year from 2022 until the two worlds converge. Giving Green starts from Vivid Economics' scenarios for ClimateWorks, makes the high-innovation world less optimistic about cultivated meat (after Rethink Priorities' forecasts) and puts the low-innovation world halfway between the original two, because alternative proteins already get public money. How long the gap lasts is Giving Green's guess (CEA!B6:D6): 15 years in the best guess, 5 in the low-impact case and 20 in the high-impact case, which is where this range comes from. The sheet's sums cover one year fewer than each guess (2022–35 is 14 years; 4 and 19 in the other cases); we keep Giving Green's values.

rows.explainer: Giving Green's bottom line: about $2.98 a tonne (range $0.68 to $192). Giving Green treats this as a rough plausibility check against its benchmark of about $1 a tonne for a top nonprofit, with low confidence.

rows.label: …is x times as cost-effective as Tradewater
Top recommendation benchmark ($ per tonne CO₂e)
rows.explainer: Giving Green's rough bar for a top nonprofit: about $1 a tonne, with anything under $10 plausibly in range.

rows.label: …is x times as cost-effective as the top recommendation benchmark
Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar
rows.explainer: One over Giving Green's cost per tonne. How much air pollution these tonnes cut is the row below.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fuel
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The tonnes are methane and nitrous oxide from animals and manure and CO₂ from clearing land for feed and pasture, none of which comes with the fine particles from burning fossil fuels behind most of the deaths in the shared climate rate. Livestock supply chains do burn some fuel (feed, processing, transport), but making alternative proteins takes energy too, so the net is near zero; the high end allows for some fuel saved and for smoke from land-clearing fires (see the Coalition for Rainforest Nations model). Methane also forms ozone, which kills; that isn't counted here (see the write-up).

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: The row the site's climate conversion reads (docs/normalization.md 2.5): the air-pollution deaths each of these tonnes avoids, as a multiple of the world average behind the shared rate, 1.46 air-pollution deaths per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ from fossil fuels (Rethink Priorities). The conversion values every tonne for its heat deaths (discounted over the decades until they come) and adds "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂"'s air-pollution part times this row, at once. Here it is the share of tonnes from burning less fuel, at the world-average smoke per tonne; at 0, the fuel doesn't matter.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Default for research, technical assistance and policy work: mostly people. Our judgment; we haven't seen this charity's breakdown.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Scientists, lawyers and policy staff could typically earn considerably more in industry, law firms or consulting. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar donated
rows.explainer: The tonnes per dollar above; with credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest). The site turns these tonnes into years of healthy life through the deaths they avoid: "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂", its heat part discounted over "Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂" for every tonne, and its air-pollution part, at once, times "Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne" above.
